segments.say: Lesson 8. Two Pointers. Opposite-end pointers on sorted data, plus same-direction read/write pointers for in-place work.

Two pointers means keeping two index variables (like l and r ) moving through an array at the same time, so one pass replaces a nested loop. Here is an analogy. Two people searching a sorted bookshelf for two books whose prices add up to ₹500: one starts at the cheap end, one at the expensive end. Too expensive? The right person steps left. Too cheap? The left person steps right.

Why does this matter? Turns many O of n squared pair problems into O of n with O of 1 extra memory. Used for sorted-array pairs, palindromes, in-place removal and merging. A few key words. Pointer: Here, just an integer index into the array. Opposite ends: l starts at 0, r at the end, moving toward each other. Same direction: A slow "write" pointer and a fast "read" pointer. Sorted: In increasing order. Many two-pointer tricks need this.

Two flavours. Opposite ends (L leads to from R): sorted arrays, pairs or triplets with a target sum, palindromes, container with most water. Each step eliminates candidates. Same direction (slow/fast, read/write): in-place filtering (remove duplicates, move zeroes), partitioning, merging two sorted arrays.
Signals. Input is sorted (or can be sorted cheaply) and you need pairs or triplets. "In place", " O of 1 extra space". Palindrome checks, reversing, comparing from both ends.
Template (opposite ends). Here is the code. Pause the video to read it line by line.

Why it is correct. With a sorted array, if a index l plus a index r is too big, a index r can't pair with anything to the right of l (those are even bigger), so discarding r is safe. Every move safely eliminates one candidate.
Let's compare. Needs sorted input?: no, yes. Time: O of n, O of n (+ O of n log n if you must sort). Extra space: O of n, O of 1. Returns original indices?: yes, only if already sorted.

Problem 1: Two Sum I I (sorted). The list numbers is sorted in increasing order. Return the 1-based positions i, j of the two numbers that add up to target, using only O of 1 extra memory. For example, with numbers equals 2, 7, 11, 15, target equals 9, the answer is 1, 2. 2 plus 7 equals 9, at positions 1 and 2 (1-based)
What is it really asking? It's Two Sum again, but sorted and without extra memory, so no dict. Sorted order is the hint for two pointers.

The obvious brute force: Two nested loops over all pairs, or a dict like in Two Sum (which uses O of n memory). That costs O of n squared time, or O of n memory. The smart way: Opposite-end pointers: too big leads to move R left, too small leads to move L right. Step by step: l equals 0, r equals last index. Then, s equals numbers index l plus numbers index r. Then, s equals target leads to answer. s less than target leads to l plus equals 1 (need bigger). s greater than target leads to r minus = 1 (need smaller).
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of 1 space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 2: 3Sum. Return all unique triplets a, b, c from the list that add up to 0. The same triplet must not appear twice. For example, with nums equals -1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4, the answer is -1, -1, 2, -1, 0, 1. Two different triplets sum to zero

The obvious brute force: Three nested loops over all triplets, plus a set to remove duplicates. That costs O of n cubed time. The smart way: Sort. Fix each anchor i, then run Two Sum I I on the rest. Skip duplicate anchors and duplicate left values to avoid repeated triplets. Step by step: Sort the list. Then, For each index i (skip it if nums index i equals the previous value), look for two numbers after i that sum to minus nums index i. Then, Use two pointers l equals i+1, r equals end, moving them like Two Sum I I. Then, On a match, record it, then move l past duplicate values.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n squared time, O of 1 extra (besides output). Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 3: Container With Most Water. You get a list of heights. Each height is a vertical line at that position. Choose two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water. Area equals distance between the lines times the shorter line's height. For example, with height equals 1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7, the answer is 49. Lines at index 1 (height 8) and 8 (height 7): width 7 times min(8, 7) equals 49

The obvious brute force: Try every pair of lines and compute each area. That costs O of n squared time. The smart way: Area equals width times shorter height. Start widest, then always move the shorter wall: moving the taller one can never help, because the height is capped by the shorter wall and the width shrinks. Step by step: Start with the widest container: l equals 0, r equals end. Then, Compute the area and keep the best. Then, Move the pointer at the shorter line inward: the shorter line limits the area, so only replacing it can help. Then, Stop when l meets r.
Let's watch it run. Widest container: limited by height 1. Move the shorter wall (L).
Area 49, the new best. R is shorter now, so move R.
Smaller. Keep moving the shorter wall (R).
Equal heights: move either. The pointers converge in O of n; the answer stays 49.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of 1 space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

A likely interview question: Why is two pointers correct on sorted input? A strong answer: Each comparison proves one endpoint can't be part of any remaining answer, so discarding it is safe. n eliminations leads to O of n.
